---
title: "Three very different roles for LLMs"
editor:
  markdown:
    wrap: sentence
---

Large language models (LLMs) --- ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and the tools built on top of them --- have changed how a great deal of data analysis gets done, including predictive analytics.
You are almost certainly already using them.
The purpose of this section is not to tell you whether to use them, but to help you think clearly about *what* you are using them for, because the answer changes the risks involved enormously.

In conversations about "using AI for predictive analytics," three completely different activities routinely get blurred together.
They deserve to be separated:

1.  **The LLM as a coding assistant.** You describe what you want in English and it writes the R code. Here the LLM changes *how the work gets done*, but it does not change what is statistically correct. Every principle in this course still applies, and --- as we will discuss --- some of the most damaging mistakes in predictive analytics are exactly the ones LLM-generated code produces most confidently.

2.  **The LLM as a way to create predictors.** You have case notes, referral narratives, intake summaries, or open-ended survey responses --- text that has never been usable in a model before. An LLM turns that text into numbers that can go into a predictor set. Here the LLM changes *what data you can use*, and this is genuinely the most promising of the three for service settings.

3.  **The LLM as the prediction model itself.** You give the LLM a person's characteristics and ask it to output a risk score. Here the LLM *replaces* the learner. This is the role that gets the most attention and is, in most service contexts, the one you should be most skeptical of.

These are not variations on a theme.
They differ in what could go wrong, in what you would have to check, and in whether the resulting system could be defended to a stakeholder or a court.
A student who says "we used AI in our predictive model" has told you almost nothing until they say which of the three they mean.

![](images/ML.jpg){fig-align="left" width="6in"}

## A framing worth holding on to

Notice that the framework this course has built --- scope the problem, specify learners, compare them against a simple benchmark, evaluate on held-out test data, examine bias, then decide about deployment --- does not need to be rebuilt to accommodate any of this.

Role 2 slots in as a new way of constructing a *predictor set*.
Role 3 slots in as a new *modeling approach*.
Both are still just [learners](poc_learners.qmd), and both still have to earn their place by beating the benchmark on data they have never seen.
That is a useful thing to remember when a vendor or a headline suggests the old rules no longer apply.

Role 1 sits outside the framework entirely, because it is about your workflow rather than your model.
It is also the one every single one of you will use, so we start there.

## Where this section sits in the course

This section comes near the end deliberately.
Almost everything worth saying about LLMs in predictive analytics depends on concepts covered earlier: [leakage and overfitting](data_overfitting.qmd), [how data are split](data_split.qmd), [calibration](perform_calibration.qmd), [bias](bias_intro.qmd), and [deployment](deployment.qmd).
Now that those are in place, we can be specific rather than hand-wavy.
